problems.title: Polynomial derivative from first principles
problems.objective: Use the definition of the derivative to compute a polynomial derivative at an arbitrary point.
problems.statement: Let $f(x)=x^2+3x$. Prove directly from the definition of the derivative that $f'(a)=2a+3$ for every $a\in\mathbb R$.
permittedResults: Definition of the derivative at a point: $f'(a)=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$, provided this limit exists.
Algebraic limit laws for finite sums and scalar multiples.
problems.strategy: Write the difference quotient at an arbitrary point $a$, expand the numerator, cancel $h$ only under the hypothesis $h\ne0$, and then apply the algebraic limit laws.
hints: Substitute $f(a+h)$ and $f(a)$ into the displayed difference quotient.
Expand $(a+h)^2$ and factor $h$ from the numerator before cancelling it.
After cancellation, the quotient is $2a+3+h$. Which term tends to zero?
problems.solution: Fix $a\in\mathbb R$. For $h\ne0$, $$\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}=\frac{(a+h)^2+3(a+h)-(a^2+3a)}{h}=\frac{2ah+h^2+3h}{h}=2a+3+h.$$ Therefore the algebraic limit laws give $$f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}(2a+3+h)=2a+3.$$ Since $a$ was arbitrary, the formula holds at every real point.
rubricCriteria: Writes the correct difference quotient at an arbitrary real point $a$.
Expands the numerator and cancels the factor $h$ only for $h\ne0$.
